scenarios.name: Magnitude 9 Cascadia earthquake
scenarios.applies_because: Coos County is on the Cascadia coast, next to the fault. Scientists put the chance of a major Cascadia earthquake near Coos Bay at about 40 in 100 over the next 50 years. Oregon asks every household to be ready for at least two weeks, so the plan includes it.
scenarios.effect_summary: Planning for it changes: Power: 10 days → 180 days; Tap water: 90 days → 365 days; Food and supplies: 30 days → 60 days; Medicine: 45 days → 90 days; Phone and payments: 10 days → 45 days.

scenarios.name: Tsunami from a nearby earthquake
scenarios.applies_because: Part of Coos County is in the tsunami zone: about 17 in 100 residents live there. After a nearby earthquake the first waves arrive in 15 to 20 minutes, so anyone who lives, works or goes to school in the zone should walk to high ground as soon as the shaking stops. Knowing the route costs nothing, so the plan includes it.
scenarios.effect_summary: Planning for it changes: households like yours that have to leave home quickly within 10 years: 16 → 18 in 100.

savings_track.why: Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (9–40) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 12 months of expenses (about $45,600); you have 3 months saved. Your supplies plan is done by month 15. After that, your $150 a month for supplies could go here, reaching the goal in about 19 years. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

requirements.plain: 2 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
26 packs of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Your generator burns about 2.8 gallons of fuel a day at light load (up to 7.1 gallons at full load): 180 days is about 504 gallons. That is more than the 25 gallons most fire codes let a home store, so keep up to 25 gallons in approved cans (10 in an attached garage, none indoors) and plan to refuel. Use stored fuel within 6 months. Run the generator outdoors only, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. (Generator spec sheet, local fire code, CDC, Ready.gov)

1 battery power station (about 1,070 Wh each) as an optional upgrade for lights, phones and a radio. Your essential load (phones) is about 30 Wh a day, 5,400 Wh for 180 days; one station gives about 910 Wh after losses, enough for about 30.3 days of that load. A full-size fridge alone would drain one in about 0.9 days. (retail prices, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: a portable generator can run the fridge, lights and the well pump through a 180-day outage. It must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage, and it needs fuel (see the fuel line). (CDC, Ready.gov, Ready Reckoner research; some amounts are estimates)

Optional for a 180-day outage: a portable solar panel with a battery. In December a 100 W panel near your latitude makes about 219 Wh a day (like Minneapolis, MN). Your essential load of about 30 Wh a day needs about 10 W of panels in full sun; a full-size fridge would need about 450 W. Panels laid flat or in shade make less. (NREL PVWatts, ENERGY STAR; some amounts are estimates)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 180 days = 179,100 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

Optional: your well pump needs about 1,250 W to run (1,000 to 1,500) and 2 to 3 times that to start; check its nameplate. At 1 hour a day that is 225,000 Wh for 180 days. A battery power station usually cannot start it; a generator or a hand pump can. Stored water is the cheaper way to cover this. (an estimate)

2 people × 1 gallon a day × 14 days = 28 gallons, plus 9.6 gallons for the 2 dogs and the cat: about 37.6 gallons. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. Your target is 365 days. Storing all of it would take about 980.9 gallons, so the plan stores the first 14 days and makes the rest safe with a filter and a water source (see the next line). (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD, Merck Veterinary Manual; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)

After day 14, for the other 351 days: make about 2.7 gallons of water safe each day, about 943.3 gallons in all, with a water filter and a source such as rain barrels, a stream or a pond, instead of storing more. Filter it, then boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. If there is no water source near you, store more water instead. (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD, Merck Veterinary Manual; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 2 people × 365 days = 329 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 2 people × 365 days = 730 cups, about 45.6 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

2 adults at about 2,262 kcal a day each: about 4,523 kcal a day × 60 days = 271,400 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $1,114 for 120 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 10 % for a household of 2). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $300 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $3,257 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $1,221 to $5,292). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

Grains: about 40.6 lb for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (wheat, white rice, rolled oats and pasta), for 2 people. Packed dry, low in oxygen and below 75 °F, wheat and white rice keep about 30 years; in a hot garage or attic, about 5. Never pack moist food without oxygen (botulism). (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)

Dry beans, peas and lentils: about 10.2 lb for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (dry beans, peas and lentils), for 2 people. Packed dry and cool, it keeps about 25 years. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)

Nonfat dry milk: about 8.1 lb for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (nonfat dry milk), for 2 people. Packed dry and cool, it keeps about 15 years. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)

Sugar: about 11.5 lb for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (sugar or other sweeteners), for 2 people. Packed dry and cool, it keeps about 30 years. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)

Dried fruit and vegetables: about 6.2 lb for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (dried apple slices, potato flakes, dried carrots and dried onions), for 2 people. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)

Salt and baking soda or powder: about 2.1 lb for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (iodized salt and baking soda and baking powder), for 2 people. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)
Cooking oil: about 0.3 gallons for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (cooking oil), for 2 people. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)

Vitamin C tablets: about 60 tablets for days 31 to 60 as bulk staples (vitamin C tablets (90 mg)), for 2 people. Staples can fall short on calcium and vitamins A, C, B12 and E; the BYU list adds vitamin C. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU, Dietary Guidelines, USU Extension; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,262 kcal a day) one lasts about 17 to 23 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

Dry food for the 2 dogs and the cat for 60 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog and 0.15 lb a day for each cat = 93 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the 2 dogs and the cat for 60 days (180 pet-days, at least a week): what they eat now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

If you cook or boil water on a camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 2 people × 60 days = 24 lb, or 48 canisters of 0.5 lb each. Use it outdoors only, never indoors (carbon monoxide). (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 2 people × 365 days = 146 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 4 person-months: 2 people × 2 months. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 1,800 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 4 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 2 people aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 4 cycles' worth, about 80 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
1 battery fan: 1 for the home. Fans help only while it is below 90 °F indoors; above that, go to a cooling centre. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
2 cooling towels, one for each person: wet them and wear them on the neck in a heat wave. (an estimate)
A heat plan: find your nearest cooling centre (dial 2-1-1), pick the coolest room, cover sunny windows, and agree who checks on whom. Never leave people or pets in a closed car. (CDC, Ready.gov)
2 warm blankets, one for each person: most homes already have them. (Ready.gov, Sphere)
2 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)
An upgrade, not a need: 2 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person. Your wood stove heats without power, so keep dry wood instead. (Ready.gov, Sphere)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Your wood stove keeps you warm as long as you have dry wood; keep the chimney clear. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 30 days of it on hand. Your target is 90 days; beyond 30 days, ask your prescriber or insurer about a longer fill. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. No agency sets a one-month amount: this step sits between the two-week advice (Red Cross, Oregon, Washington) and the Church's three-month pantry. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 2 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 180 days without power = 5,400 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 two-way radios for the 2 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
2 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 14 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

2 go-bags, one for each person: a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 2 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 2 gallons a day for the 2 people × 2 days = 4 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 4,523 kcal a day × 2 days = 9,000 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

3 pet carriers, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine each takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the 2 dogs and the cat = 4.8 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD, Merck Veterinary Manual; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the 2 dogs and the cat = 30 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)
Keep both vehicles at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. (Ready.gov)

Person 1 travels 7.5 miles (12 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 2.5 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 1's walk home: 2.5 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 1.2 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 300 kcal for 2.5 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)
2 car emergency kits: jumper cables, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 2 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

3 packages of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and a laxative): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 12 packages for 60 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

N95 masks for wildfire smoke or an outbreak: 1 a day for each of the 2 people aged 4 and over, for 5 days = 10 masks. A well-fitting N95 protects more than a cloth or surgical mask. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 2 people and 60 days that is 26 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. If anyone sleeps upstairs, check that each bedroom has a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder. Test your smoke alarms every month. (Ready.gov)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

Savings goal: about 12 months of expenses ($45,600 at $3,800 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 3 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)
A standard home policy does not cover earthquake damage. Decide whether earthquake insurance is worth its deductible where you live. (Ready.gov)

# Your preparedness packet

**For:** 2 adults, with 2 dogs and 1 cat  
**Where:** Coos County, Oregon (ZIP code 97420)  
**Home:** an owned house, with a private well, a wood stove, no air conditioning and a generator  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** rare catastrophes, the kind that come about once in 500 years (the 1-in-500 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** one year of supplies; each need stops at the step that covers it. At your budget, the plan gets there by month 15 (January 2028).

### The three things that matter most

1. Of 100 households like yours, about 50 (40–90) will lose grid power for a day or more in the next 10 years. Be ready to manage about 6 months at home with no power, and about 1 year with no tap water.
2. Of 100 households like yours, about 55 (35–90) will be unable to shop for food and supplies for 3 days or more in the next 10 years. Keep about 2 months of food you normally eat, and 3 months of daily medicine on hand.
3. Your longest targets come from one event the plan includes: a magnitude 9 Cascadia earthquake. Planning for it changes: Power: 10 days → 180 days; Tap water: 90 days → 365 days; Food and supplies: 30 days → 60 days; Medicine: 45 days → 90 days; Phone and payments: 10 days → 45 days. You can turn it off on the risks screen to see the plan without it.

### Start here

These cost nothing and come first. This month's 8 free steps are all under Your plan.

- [ ] Keep medicines going: a written list, early refills, an emergency supply
- [ ] Tap water in clean reused bottles
- [ ] Fire safety at home: alarms, an escape plan, safe cooking and heating

### What the plan assumes you already have

- [x] A charged mobile phone: alerts, calls and a backup light (2 phones)
- [x] Go-bag for each person: a backpack you pack from your supplies (2 bags)
- [x] Manual can opener (1 opener)
- [x] A cooking pot with a lid (1 pot)
- [x] Three days of the food you normally eat (2 × 3 days of food for one person)
- [x] A warm blanket for each person (2 blankets)
- [x] Warm layers for each person: a coat, hat and gloves (2 sets)
- [x] Towels to wet and cool down (2 towels)

Most homes have these, so the plan does not ask you to buy them. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen, or list the item as not owned, and the plan will add it.

## Your risks

The events most likely to reach a household like yours in Coos County, Oregon, over the next 10 years, most likely first. A lost job or a week-long outage is far more likely than a disaster from the movies, and the plan is ordered the same way.

### The ones most likely to reach you

#### 1. Strong wind

Nearly every household like yours will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years (about 1.1 times a year).[2, 3]

**What helps.** Pick your shelter spot now. A safe room or storm shelter is best. The next best is a small, windowless room or basement on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.[4] Sign up for your community's warnings, and learn what your sirens sound like.[4] Know the signs of a tornado: a rotating funnel cloud, a cloud of debris, or a roar like a freight train. In your shelter, protect your head and neck with your arms, and pile blankets or cushions around you.[4] When thunder roars, go indoors. Get into a building or a car with a roof.[5]

**What to avoid.** Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls.[4] There is no safe place in a car during a tornado, only less dangerous ones. If you are caught, stay buckled in and keep your head below the windows.[4] During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and electronics plugged into the wall.[5]

**What it can do:** no power, no phone, internet or card payments and damage to the home. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Rough data.

#### 2. Medical emergency

Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years.[6, 7]

**What helps.** Take a first-aid and bleeding-control class. You may be able to save a life by acting right after an injury, before help arrives.[8] Keep a stocked first-aid kit. Check it regularly and replace anything used or out of date.[9] Keep a list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies with your emergency supplies.[10] Know how to reach 911. Call if you can, and text where that service works.[11] Set up telehealth with your own clinician before you need it.[12]

**What to avoid.** Do not start antibiotics on your own or take someone else's. The wrong medicine can delay the right treatment and cause serious side effects.[13] Do not use expired medicines.[14]

**What it can do:** a medical emergency. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 3. Cold wave

Of 100 households like yours, about 96 will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years.[2]

**What helps.** Keep extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats, and pick one room to keep warm.[15] Learn how to keep pipes from freezing, and test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms before winter.[16] Keep a car kit with jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, water and snacks, and keep the gas tank full.[16] Check on older neighbours often.[15] Know the signs of hypothermia, such as shivering, confusion and slurred speech. A body temperature below 95°F is an emergency. Warm the center of the body first.[16] In avalanche country, get training, sign up for alerts from a Forest Service avalanche center, and carry a beacon, a probe and a small shovel.[17]

**What to avoid.** Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Use generators and grills only outdoors, away from windows.[16] Choose electric space heaters with automatic shut-off, and keep them 3 feet from anything that can burn.[15, 18] Do not overdo it when you shovel snow.[16]

**What it can do:** no power, no tap water and dangerous heat or cold at home. **How bad:** Moderate. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 4. Heat wave

Of 100 households like yours, about 95 will go through a heat wave in the next ten years.[2]

**What helps.** Know where you can go to cool off. Dial 2-1-1 to find air conditioning near you.[19] Cover windows with drapes or shades, and weather-strip doors and windows.[20] Take cool showers, wear loose, light-colored clothing, and drink plenty of fluids. Check on family members, older adults and neighbours.[20] Heat can cause power outages, so plan for refrigerated medicines and powered medical devices.[19] In a drought, follow local limits on water use, and make saving water a daily habit.[21]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on a fan when it is over 90°F indoors. It can make you hotter.[19] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day. Heat stroke is an emergency. Signs include a body temperature above 103°F, hot, red, dry skin, a fast pulse and confusion. Call 911.[20]

**What it can do:** no power and dangerous heat or cold at home. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Based on data.

#### 5. Stranded in a vehicle

Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.[3, 22]

**What helps.** Keep a car kit with jumper cables, sand, a flashlight, warm clothes, blankets, water and snacks.[16] Keep the gas tank at least half full.[23] Check the pressure in all your tires, including the spare, at least once a month.[24] Before a winter trip, tell someone where you are going and when you expect to arrive, and ask them to call for help if you are late.[15] If you drive an electric car, know its range and where you can charge along your route.[25, 26]

**What to avoid.** If you are stuck in a snowstorm, staying in the car is often safest. Tie a bright cloth to the antenna. Run the engine about 10 minutes an hour with a window open a little, and keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow.[15] Never drive into a flooded road or around the barriers.[27]

**What it can do:** being stranded away from home. **How bad:** Minor. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 6. Job loss

Of 100 households like yours, about 92 (77–99) will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.[3, 28, 29]

**What helps.** Build an emergency fund a little at a time. The right amount depends on your situation.[30] Planners often suggest three to six months of living expenses, and more if your income varies.[31] Know how to file for unemployment in your state.[32] Keep copies of your financial, legal and medical papers together, with the names of people to call.[33] Write a bare-bones budget you could switch to, and keep a pantry that can stretch a tight month.

**What to avoid.** Do not wait to file. Contact your state's unemployment program as soon as possible after losing work.[32] Do not keep your emergency fund in investments you would have to sell. A savings account lets you take money out at any time without a penalty.[31]

**What it can do:** lost income. **How bad:** Serious. **How sure:** Mostly data.

#### 7. Earthquake

Of 100 households like yours, about 11 will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.[34, 35]

**What helps.** Practice Drop, Cover and Hold On: drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops.[36] Secure bookcases, water heaters, TVs and other heavy things, and keep heavy objects on low shelves. A standard homeowner's policy does not cover earthquake damage.[36] Store water in case the taps stop. On the coast, the shaking is your warning. As soon as it stops, walk to high ground or inland without waiting for an alert.[37] A loud roar from the ocean, or water that suddenly drains away, is another sign.[38] Near a volcano, leave early if you are told to. Ash can travel hundreds of miles, so keep N95 masks.[39]

**What to avoid.** Do not run outside during shaking, and stay away from doorways.[36] Do not go back to the shore until officials say it is safe. Tsunami waves can keep coming for hours.[37] Avoid driving in heavy ash.[39]

**What it can do:** no power, no tap water, no way to get to a store, gaps in medicine, no phone, internet or card payments, a medical emergency and damage to the home. **How bad:** Very severe. **How sure:** Mostly data.

### No grid power at home: about 6 months (2 months to 1 year)

**What helps.** Have a flashlight for each person.[56] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio, and a backup battery for each phone.[57] Keep the fridge and freezer closed. A closed fridge keeps food cold for about four hours, and a full freezer for about two days.[56] If someone relies on a powered medical device or cold medicine, make a plan with their medical provider now.[56] You can also ask your power company to put you on its list for priority restoration.[10] A battery power station burns no fuel, so it makes no carbon monoxide.[58]

**What to avoid.** Never run a generator inside your home or garage, even with the doors and windows open. Keep it outside, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.[58] Put a carbon monoxide alarm on every level of your home.[56] Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Unplug electronics, because the power can come back with a surge that damages them.[56]

### No tap water at all: about 1 year (6 months to 1 year)

**What helps.** Store at least one gallon per person per day, for drinking and keeping clean.[1] Fill clean bottles or jugs with tap water and replace it every six months.[59] You can pick a level in the plan. About 3 liters a day covers drinking to survive, one gallon is the basic default, and about 4 gallons (15 liters) is the humanitarian minimum for drinking, cooking and washing.[60] A tank water heater holds 20 to 80 gallons of clean water.[61, 62] For long outages, a filter and a source of raw water go further than more jugs.[55] Filters do not remove viruses, so add a disinfectant such as chlorine dioxide after filtering.[63] A two-bucket toilet keeps waste safe when toilets cannot flush.[64]

**What to avoid.** Do not store water in containers that held chemicals.[59] Milk jugs seal poorly and turn brittle.[65] Never drink pool or spa water. Use it only for washing and cleaning.[62]

### Can't get to a store: about 2 months (1½–6)

**What helps.** Keep extra food that needs no refrigeration, cooking or water, and choose foods your family will eat.[66] Use the oldest cans first and replace them as you go.[67] Buy a little at a time. Ready.gov asks people to buy supplies slowly, so everyone can get what they need.[68] Keep a manual can opener.[66] The plan counts food in calories, not servings. Many "30-day" meal kits hold only about 1,300 to 1,700 calories a day.[69] That is less than most adults need.[70] Store food somewhere cool and dry. Below 85°F is best.[67]

**What to avoid.** Do not buy everything at once. It strains your budget and the store. Do not buy or eat from cans that bulge, leak, are rusted or are deeply dented.[67] Do not trust a kit's "days" label. Check the calories on the package instead.

### Dangerous heat or cold indoors: about 2 weeks (10 days to 2 weeks)

**What helps.** Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone.[15, 19] In heat, go where there is air conditioning. Dial 2-1-1 to find one.[19] Cover windows with drapes or shades.[20] In cold, close off rooms you don't need, stuff towels under doors, and cover windows with blankets at night. Have extra blankets, sleeping bags and warm coats.[15] Babies under one year old should never sleep in a cold room.[15]

**What to avoid.** Fans move air but do not lower body temperature.[20] Above 90°F indoors, a fan can make you hotter.[19] Never heat your home with a gas oven, and never use a grill or camp stove indoors.[58] Keep space heaters 3 feet from anything that can burn.[18] Never leave people or pets in a closed car on a warm day.[20]

### Medication and medical-supply continuity: about 3 months (1½–6)

**What helps.** Refill early, while you still have a week left. The Red Cross suggests keeping a 7-day supply, and Florida advises at least two weeks.[71, 72] People with diabetes should pack supplies for at least 1 to 2 weeks.[73] Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about building an emergency supply, and keep a written list of each person's medicines, doses and allergies.[10] Many states let pharmacists give an emergency refill, but the rules differ from state to state.[74] After a declared disaster, a federal program can help people without insurance replace prescriptions.[75] If a medicine must stay cold, ask how long it can be kept warm, and plan a cooler.[56]

**What to avoid.** If the power is out for more than a day, throw away medicine that should be refrigerated, unless the label says otherwise.[56] Keep insulin cool but never frozen.[76] Do not use expired medicines. Weak antibiotics can fail to treat an infection.[14] Do not share antibiotics or save them for later.[13]

### No phone, internet or card payments: about 1½ months (3 weeks to 3 months)

**What helps.** Turn on emergency alerts on every phone. They are free, and you do not need to sign up.[77] Keep a battery or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with a tone alert.[57] NOAA Weather Radio has more than 1,000 transmitters covering all 50 states.[78] Write important phone numbers on paper, not only in your phone.[79] Pick an out-of-state contact everyone can text, and a place to meet if you are separated.[36] Keep some cash in small bills, because ATMs and credit cards may not work.[80] License-free two-way radios (FRS) let family members talk over short distances without a phone network.[81]

**What to avoid.** Do not rely on one source of news. Do not assume you can text 911 everywhere. It is not available in every area, so call 911 if you can.[11]

**What to avoid.** Many people wait to check with others before they act on a warning.[82] Always follow the instructions of local officials, and leave early enough to avoid being trapped by bad weather.[23] Never walk or drive through floodwater. Six inches of moving water can knock you down.[83]

### House fire

**What helps.** Put smoke alarms inside and outside sleeping areas and on every level of your home. Test them every month.[84] Make an escape plan with two ways out of each room, and practice it twice a year.[85] Cooking left alone is the top cause of kitchen fires that spread beyond the pan, so stay with your cooking. Keep a pan lid or baking sheet nearby to cover a pan that catches fire.[86] Keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from heaters, fireplaces and candles.[18] A multipurpose extinguisher labeled "A-B-C" works on most home fires.[87]

**What to avoid.** If a person or pet is still inside, get out, call 911, and tell firefighters where they are.[85] Never heat your home with an oven.[18] Turn off space heaters when you leave the room or go to bed.[18] Replace 9-volt alarm batteries at least once a year.[84]

### Home and personal security

**What helps.** Burglars look for homes that are easy targets. Lock up, and light the places where someone could hide.[88] Work with your neighbours to look out for each other.[88] Protect key accounts with a password manager and two-step login.[89] Learn a simple way to handle a tense moment: notice what is happening, say hello, judge the risk, and get help if you need it.[90] If an attack happens in a public place, getting away is the top priority.[91]

**What to avoid.** After a disaster, be careful with people who show up offering fast repairs or help for a fee. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[92] Do not hide a spare key under the doormat or a planter. Leave it with a trusted neighbour.[88]

### Contacts and meeting places

- **Make a household plan and a contact card for each person.** Agree how you will reach each other, where you will meet if you are separated, and who picks up the children (Ready.gov). Pick one out-of-state contact everyone texts to say they are safe, since texts often get through when calls do not, and write key numbers on a card for each wallet or bag (Ready.gov). Add school, daycare and work plans, and go over the plan together once a year.[33, 36, 79, 99, 103, 104]
- **Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911.** Make sure every phone can get warnings: Wireless Emergency Alerts are free and need no sign-up (Ready.gov), but a phone only gets them when it is on, not in airplane mode, and served by a carrier that takes part (FCC). Add your county's text and email alerts and your power company's outage texts for local news. Call 911 when you can, because texting 911 works only in some places (FCC).[11, 56, 77, 103, 105]

### Leaving home: triggers and routes

About 20 of 100 households like yours have to leave home quickly at least once in 10 years. Warning can be 1 minute to 12 hours ahead. Plan to be away for about 2 days.[3, 35, 37, 40, 41, 46, 47, 48]

- **Plan how you would leave: zone, routes, destination and triggers.** Look up your evacuation zone and routes on your state and county emergency management websites, mark two routes on a paper map, and pick where you would go, pet-friendly if you have pets (Ready.gov). For each likely hazard, write a go-or-stay card and an if-then trigger, such as 'If our zone gets an evacuation warning, we leave within 30 minutes.' Plans written in if-then form make people more likely to follow through.[23, 57, 82, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110]
- **Keep your vehicle ready: half a tank, a charged battery, a good spare.** Keep at least half a tank of gas at all times and a full tank when an evacuation looks likely (Ready.gov); if you drive an electric car, keep it charged through storm season and pick destinations within its range (Hillsborough County, Florida). Check the spare tire with the others each month, and keep a phone charging cable in the car (NHTSA). Run the engine only outdoors, never in a garage (CDC).[16, 23, 24, 25, 26, 58, 97, 111]

- **Practice: ten-minute drills and the first things to do.**

#### Drills and if-then plans

**If-then plans.** An if-then plan links a trigger to an action: "If the county issues an evacuation warning for our zone, we leave within 30 minutes." Plans written this way help people follow through.[109] When a warning comes, people often wait to confirm it with others before they act.[82] A trigger you agreed on earlier leaves less to decide in the moment. Write one for each likely hazard, and add who picks up the children and where you will meet.[103]

**Drills.** In New Zealand, people who took part in earthquake drills knew the right actions better, used them more during real shaking, and did more to prepare.[112] Among people who got out of the World Trade Center on 9/11, those with earlier emergency training were less likely to develop PTSD.[113] Practice your fire escape plan twice a year.[85] Other ten-minute drills: Drop, Cover and Hold On, a night without power, grabbing the go-bag against a timer, and sealing a room to shelter in place.[110]

**What to avoid.** Do not skip drills because they feel silly. Each one you finish counts toward your plan.

The household plan above covers school, daycare and work plans and a walking route home. Each commuter's get-home bag is under Checklists.

### Neighbors

- **Neighbours and skills: swap numbers, check on each other, learn first aid.**

#### Neighbours and mutual aid

**The gap.** About 7 in 10 people expect help from friends and family in a disaster, but fewer than 2 in 10 had heard how to help their neighbours.[114]

**What helps.** Swap phone numbers with two neighbours. Agree who checks on whom, especially older neighbours and anyone who lives alone. Make a simple contact list for your street. Give a trusted person a spare key, and tell them where your supplies are and how to use any medical equipment.[115] Host a block party, since strong communities start with prepared neighbours.[116] Take CERT training to learn fire safety, light search and rescue, and disaster first aid.[117]

**What to avoid.** Do not wait for a disaster to meet the people next door. A short hello now makes it easier to knock on a door later.

### Pets

- **Pet plan: microchip, records, a photo and a buddy.** Keep your pet's ID tag and microchip details current, put vaccination records and a recent photo with your documents, and arrange a buddy who can care for or evacuate your pets if you cannot (Ready.gov). If officials ask you to evacuate, your pets should go too.[107, 108]

## Documents and money

Keep paper copies in a waterproof pouch and photos you can reach from any phone. FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit groups them in four parts.[33]

- [ ] **Who you are:** photo IDs, birth certificates, Social Security cards, passports, and pet records.
- [ ] **Money and legal papers:** insurance policies, the lease or deed, bank and card contact numbers (not PINs), and recent tax returns.
- [ ] **Medical papers:** insurance cards, the written medicine list, prescriptions, and vaccination records.
- [ ] **Contacts:** family, doctors, the insurance agent, the landlord or lender, and employers.

- **Documents and insurance: copy key papers, record belongings, check cover.** Use FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit to gather IDs, financial and legal papers, insurance, medical information and contacts, and photograph or video every room and valuable item. Keep paper copies in a waterproof bag and another copy with someone you trust or in secure online storage (FEMA). Check what your insurance covers: standard home and renters policies do not cover flood or earthquake damage, a new flood policy usually takes 30 days to start, and renters can buy their own policy and contents-only flood cover (Ready.gov, FEMA).[33, 36, 57, 80, 83, 114, 118, 119]
- **Fire-resistant, waterproof document pouch.** A fire-resistant, water-resistant pouch or small case for paper copies of key documents, a USB drive and some cash, easy to grab when you leave (FEMA's financial kit suggests fire- and waterproof storage).[33, 102]

### Insurance questions

- Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)[80, 118, 119]
- A standard home policy does not cover earthquake damage. Decide whether earthquake insurance is worth its deductible where you live. (Ready.gov)[36]

### Cash

- Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $100 to start, or enough for about 14 days of basics (food, fuel, medicine) at your own daily spending. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)[3, 33, 35, 80, 93, 94, 95, 97]

### Savings

Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (9–40) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 12 months of expenses (about $45,600); you have 3 months saved. Your supplies plan is done by month 15. After that, your $150 a month for supplies could go here, reaching the goal in about 19 years. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

- **Money: start an emergency fund and a bare-bones budget.** Set up an automatic transfer, however small, into a savings account you keep for emergencies; the CFPB says the right amount depends on your situation, and planners often suggest working toward three to six months of expenses (FINRA). Write down your essential monthly costs and what you would cut first, so you know how far savings would stretch. If anyone earns, find your state's unemployment website now, so you could file right away if a job ends (Department of Labor).[28, 30, 31, 32, 120, 121]

## Special needs

### Medicine

- 1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 30 days of it on hand. Your target is 90 days; beyond 30 days, ask your prescriber or insurer about a longer fill. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. No agency sets a one-month amount: this step sits between the two-week advice (Red Cross, Oregon, Washington) and the Church's three-month pantry. (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)[3, 35, 44, 45, 47, 71, 72, 73, 74, 93, 94, 95, 122, 123, 124]

- **Keep medicines going: a written list, early refills, an emergency supply.** Write a paper list of each person's medicines with the dose their prescriber set, allergies, and the prescriber's and pharmacy's numbers, and keep copies in the go-bag and with your documents (Ready.gov). If anyone takes a daily medicine, refill when a week is left and ask the prescriber and pharmacist how to build an emergency supply; some states allow emergency refills, and a federal program can help people without insurance after a disaster. Set up telehealth and pharmacy logins now, and put spare glasses in the go-bag (Ready.gov).[10, 12, 14, 33, 57, 71, 74, 75, 122]

### Antibiotics

- No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)[13, 14, 125, 126]

### Pets and animals

- Dry food for the 2 dogs and the cat for 60 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog and 0.15 lb a day for each cat = 93 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)[2, 3, 35, 44, 45, 93, 94, 95, 97, 107, 108, 127]
- 3 pet carriers, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine each takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)[23, 108]
- Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the 2 dogs and the cat = 4.8 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD, Merck Veterinary Manual; some amounts are estimates)[97, 108, 128, 129]
- Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the 2 dogs and the cat = 30 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)[108]

### Stress and mental health

#### Stress, mental health and the 988 line

**What helps.** Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.[130] After a disaster, the Disaster Distress Helpline offers crisis counseling 24/7 to anyone in emotional distress. Call or text 1-800-985-5990.[131] Write a short calm plan: what you might feel, what helps you, and who you will call.[110] Oregon's 2 Weeks Ready program even includes practicing mindfulness as a step in getting prepared.[93]

**What to avoid.** Do not keep the news on all day. No one, adult or child, benefits from graphic details or disturbing images.[132] Do not wait until things feel unbearable to reach out. The 988 line supports people in emotional distress as well as in crisis.[130]
